items.prompt: Which type of atomic bonding is characteristic of metals?

options.label: Covalent network bonding
Ionic bonding
Metallic bonding
Van der Waals bonding

rubric: Metals bond through a shared sea of delocalised electrons, which is metallic bonding.
Ionic bonding is a common mix-up, but it occurs between metals and non-metals.

items.prompt: What does Young's modulus measure?

options.label: Resistance to surface scratching
Stiffness in elastic deformation
Stress at which yielding begins
Energy absorbed before fracture

rubric: Young's modulus is the slope of the elastic region of the stress-strain curve, which measures stiffness.
Yield strength, toughness and hardness are separate properties that learners often confuse with it.

items.prompt: Which of these metals has a face-centred cubic (FCC) crystal structure at room temperature?

options.label: Copper
Iron (as ferrite)
Chromium
Zinc

rubric: Copper is FCC.
Chromium and room-temperature iron are BCC, and zinc is HCP.

items.prompt: What defines a thermoplastic polymer?

options.label: It sets permanently the first time it is heated
It is made only from natural rubber latex
It has a fully crystalline structure throughout
It softens on heating and can be reshaped

rubric: Thermoplastics have no permanent cross-links, so they soften and can be remelted.
Hardening permanently on heating describes a thermoset, which learners often mix up with a thermoplastic.

items.prompt: Steel is an alloy of iron with which main alloying element?

options.label: Aluminium
Carbon
Copper
Nickel

rubric: Steel is iron with small amounts of carbon, typically under about 2%.
Nickel is added to some steels but is not the defining element.

items.prompt: Which of the following are ceramic materials? Select all that apply.

options.label: Alumina (aluminium oxide)
Brass
Stainless steel
Polyethylene
Silicon carbide

rubric: Alumina and silicon carbide are inorganic, non-metallic compounds, which makes them ceramics.
Polyethylene is a polymer, and brass and stainless steel are metal alloys.

items.prompt: A designer is comparing a glass plate and a steel plate for a protective cover. The cover may be hit by flying debris. She needs the term for the energy a material can absorb before it fractures. Which property term is this?

options.label: Stiffness
Ductility
Toughness
Hardness

rubric: Toughness is the energy absorbed per unit volume up to fracture.
Ductility is how far a material stretches, and hardness and stiffness measure other things.

items.prompt: Why do metals conduct electricity well?

options.label: Their nuclei release electrons when they are heated
Their outer electrons are delocalised and free to move
Their ions can move freely through the solid
Their atoms share electrons in fixed directional bonds

rubric: Delocalised valence electrons carry charge through the metal.
Ions in a solid metal are fixed in the lattice, so ion movement does not carry the current.

items.prompt: Why are ceramics typically brittle at room temperature?

options.label: Strong directional bonds resist dislocation motion, so cracks spread
Their free electrons let atoms shift past each other, so cracks spread
Their bonds are weak, so layers slide apart under small loads
Their atoms are arranged randomly, which weakens most bonds

rubric: Ionic and covalent bonds hold atoms in place, which prevents plastic slip, so cracks grow instead.
Weak bonds are the wrong explanation, since ceramics have very strong bonds.

items.prompt: Why does cold working (for example rolling or drawing at room temperature) make a metal stronger?

options.label: It heats grain boundaries until they fuse the grains together
It adds dislocations that tangle and block each other
It converts the metal into a harder ceramic-like phase
It removes dislocations so the crystal planes slip less often

rubric: Plastic deformation multiplies dislocations, which interfere with each other, so more stress is needed for further slip.
Removing dislocations describes annealing, which softens the metal.

items.prompt: Why can a thermoset such as epoxy not be melted and reshaped after curing?

options.label: Its chains are too short and light to flow at any temperature
Its crystals are so large that they only melt above the burning point
Its weak van der Waals forces strengthen when it is reheated
Cross-links form a covalent network that stops chains sliding

rubric: Curing creates covalent cross-links between chains, so the material degrades rather than flows when heated.
Short chains are not the cause, because thermoset behaviour comes from the cross-linking.

items.prompt: In a carbon-fibre/epoxy composite, what are the main roles of the fibres and the matrix?

options.label: Both carry load equally, and neither affects the shape
The fibres give electrical insulation, and the matrix gives stiffness
The fibres carry most of the load, and the matrix holds them and passes load between them
The fibres bind the part together and fix its shape, and the matrix is the stiff phase that carries most of the load

rubric: Stiff, strong fibres carry the load, and the matrix supports them and transfers stress.
The reversed roles in the first option are a common mix-up.

items.prompt: Which of the following generally increase the strength of a metal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Work hardening
Adding alloying elements that distort the lattice
Reducing grain size
Heating it close to its melting point
Annealing at high temperature for a long time

rubric: Finer grains, solute atoms and dislocation build-up all obstruct dislocation motion.
Annealing and heating near the melting point soften the metal.

items.prompt: A cable maker coats copper wire with PVC. The copper carries current, while the PVC stops it reaching the user. A trainee asks why PVC is an insulator when copper is a conductor. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: PVC is much thicker than copper, so electrons cannot get through it
PVC's atoms are much heavier than copper's, so electrons cannot move past them
PVC's electrons are held in covalent bonds, so none are free to move
PVC's electrons are all tied to single atoms, so none can be shared between them

rubric: In polymers the valence electrons are localised in covalent bonds, so no mobile charge carriers exist.
The claim that PVC has no electrons is wrong, since it has electrons but they are bound.

items.prompt: Why can most metals be bent permanently without fracturing?

options.label: Covalent bonds stretch elastically to large strains and hold the new shape
Ionic bonds reform instantly between opposite ions after each bend
Layers of atoms slip past each other while free electrons keep bonding intact
Atoms sit in random positions, so no planes exist to resist deformation

rubric: Metallic bonding is non-directional, so atomic planes can slip without breaking the bonding.
Distractors apply ionic or covalent bonding behaviour to metals.

items.prompt: Why do ceramics usually fracture with almost no plastic deformation?

options.label: Free electrons carry stress to flaws, so cracks spread under small loads
Long tangled chains cannot untangle, so they snap when pulled hard
Weak bonds between atoms let cracks run through the structure at very low stress
Strong directional bonds resist dislocation motion, so cracks grow, not yield

rubric: Ionic/covalent bonds are strong and directional, so slip is very hard and flaws grow into cracks.
Distractors wrongly describe ceramic bonds as weak or invoke polymer chains or free electrons.

items.prompt: Why can a thermoplastic be reheated and reshaped, while a thermoset cannot?

options.label: Thermoplastics are fully crystalline and melt sharply, while thermosets are amorphous and only soften
Thermoplastic chains are held by weak secondary bonds that loosen, while thermosets have covalent crosslinks
Thermoplastics have covalent crosslinks that break and reform on heating, while thermosets rely on weak bonds
Thermoplastics have shorter chains that slide freely, while thermosets have chains too long to move

rubric: Heating weakens secondary bonds in thermoplastics, while crosslinks in thermosets stay fixed.
The strongest distractor reverses the bonding in the two polymer types.

items.prompt: Why does reducing grain size usually raise the yield strength of a metal?

options.label: Smaller grains remove all dislocations, so the metal becomes a perfect crystal
Grain boundaries block dislocation motion, so more stress is needed to keep slip going
Smaller grains make atoms bond more strongly, raising bond energy inside each grain
Boundaries melt slightly and bind neighbouring grains, filling gaps in the structure

rubric: Grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation glide (Hall-Petch strengthening).
Distractors imagine changes to bond strength or dislocation removal that do not occur.

items.prompt: Copper conducts electricity far better than alumina mainly because:

options.label: its bonds are ionic, so ions migrate freely through the solid
its crystal has fewer grains, so electrons never meet any boundary
its valence electrons are delocalised and free to move under an electric field
its atoms are heavier, so they carry charge more easily through the lattice

rubric: Metallic bonding gives a sea of mobile electrons; alumina's electrons are tightly bound.
Distractors attribute conduction to mass, ion migration or grain count.

items.prompt: Which of these processes typically increase the yield strength of a metal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cold working it by rolling at room temperature
Annealing it at high temperature for a long time
Heating it until dislocations are removed
Refining its grain size during processing
Adding alloying atoms that form a solid solution

rubric: Cold work, solid-solution atoms and finer grains all hinder dislocation motion.
Annealing and long high-temperature heating remove dislocations and soften the metal.

items.prompt: A technician bends a steel wire back and forth at one spot. At first it bends easily, but each bend feels stiffer, and after many cycles the wire snaps at that spot. Which explanation best accounts for the growing stiffness?

options.label: Bending removes free electrons, so metallic bonding strengthens locally
Heat from bending anneals the wire and refines its grains at the bend
The steel gradually converts into a ceramic at the bend, which resists deformation
Dislocations multiply and tangle, so further slip needs higher stress (work hardening)

rubric: Plastic deformation raises dislocation density, causing work hardening and eventual loss of ductility.
Annealing would soften the wire, so that distractor reverses the effect.

items.prompt: A round steel rod of 5 mm diameter carries a tensile load of 10 kN. What is the approximate tensile stress?

options.label: 2037 MPa
509 MPa
400 MPa
255 MPa

rubric: Area = pi*d^2/4 = 19.6 mm^2, so stress = 10000 N / 19.6 mm^2 = 509 MPa.
Distractors come from using a square area, a doubled area or a wrong radius.

items.prompt: Steel has a Young's modulus of 200 GPa. A bar is loaded elastically to 300 MPa. What is the strain?
rubric: Strain = stress / E = 300 MPa / 200000 MPa = 0.0015.
Other options come from unit slips (powers of ten) or inverting the ratio.

items.prompt: A 2 m aluminium bar (thermal expansion coefficient 23e-6 per K) is heated by 50 K and is free to expand. By how much does it lengthen?

options.label: 4.6 mm
23 mm
2.3 mm

rubric: Change in length = alpha * L * dT = 23e-6 * 2 m * 50 = 2.3 mm.
Distractors reflect unit errors or doubling the length.

items.prompt: Which material is the best choice for household electrical wire that must conduct well and be drawn and bent easily?

options.label: PTFE polymer
Cast iron
Copper
Alumina ceramic

rubric: Copper combines high conductivity with ductility from metallic bonding.
Alumina and PTFE are insulators; cast iron is brittle and conducts poorly.

items.prompt: A steel tool has been quenched from high temperature and is now very hard but too brittle. Which next step best reduces the brittleness while keeping most of the hardness?

options.label: Quench it again in cold water to refine the grain
Cold work it by hammering to relieve internal stress
Temper it by reheating to a moderate temperature
Anneal it by heating and cooling slowly in the furnace

rubric: Tempering relieves stress in quenched martensite, trading a little hardness for toughness.
Full annealing would remove most hardness; re-quenching or hammering adds brittleness.

items.prompt: A furnace lining must stay stable and keep its strength at 1400 C. Which materials are suitable choices? Select all that apply.

options.label: Polyethylene
Silicon carbide
Aluminium alloy
Alumina

rubric: Alumina and silicon carbide are refractory ceramics with very high melting points.
Polyethylene and aluminium alloy melt or soften far below 1400 C.

items.prompt: A steel tie rod has a yield strength of 350 MPa and a cross-section of 400 mm^2. It carries a steady tensile load of 70 kN. What is the factor of safety against yielding?
rubric: Stress = 70000 N / 400 mm^2 = 175 MPa, so factor of safety = 350 / 175 = 2.0.
Distractors invert the ratio, report the stress, or make an arithmetic slip.

items.prompt: A steel rod (E = 200 GPa) has diameter 10 mm and length 2 m. It carries an axial tensile load of 15.7 kN and stays elastic. What is its elongation?

options.label: 0.5 mm
2.0 mm
8.0 mm
0.2 mm

rubric: Area = 78.5 mm^2, stress = 200 MPa, strain = 0.001, so elongation = 2 mm.
Using the diameter as the radius gives 0.5 mm.

items.prompt: A Cu-Ni alloy with 50 wt% Ni is held at a temperature where the tie line gives a liquid of 40 wt% Ni and a solid of 55 wt% Ni. What mass fraction of the alloy is liquid?
rubric: 67% is the solid fraction, from taking the wrong arm of the lever.

items.prompt: An aluminium bar (E = 70 GPa, expansion coefficient 23e-6 per K) is rigidly clamped at both ends at 20 C. It is then heated to 70 C. What stress develops in the bar?

options.label: 80 MPa tensile
80 MPa compressive
1.6 MPa compressive
160 MPa compressive

rubric: Stress = E x alpha x dT = 70,000 MPa x 23e-6 x 50 = about 80 MPa, compressive because expansion is blocked.
Tensile ignores the direction of the blocked expansion; 1.6 MPa uses a 1 K change.

items.prompt: A tie rod must carry 50 kN in tension. The steel has a yield strength of 250 MPa and the design requires a safety factor of 2 on yield. What is the minimum cross-sectional area?
rubric: Allowable stress = 250/2 = 125 MPa, so A = 50,000 N / 125 MPa = 400 mm^2.
200 mm^2 ignores the safety factor; 100 mm^2 multiplies it instead of dividing.

items.prompt: A 0.8 wt% C steel part was austenitised and water quenched. It is very hard but chips under light impact. Which next step fits the purpose of improving its toughness?

options.label: Normalise it by air cooling from above the eutectoid so that hardness reaches its maximum
Cool it to cryogenic temperature so that remaining martensite turns into soft pearlite
Reheat it above the eutectoid temperature and quench again to refine the martensite further
Reheat it below the eutectoid temperature, hold, and cool, trading some hardness for toughness

rubric: Tempering below the eutectoid temperature lets carbon precipitate and relieves stress, which improves toughness.
Requenching or cryogenic cooling does not toughen martensite, and normalising gives softer pearlite rather than maximum hardness.

items.prompt: A sheet of annealed low-carbon steel is too soft for a bracket and must have a higher yield strength without changing its composition. Which processing steps would raise it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Holding the sheet at 700 C for hours so the grains recrystallise and grow
Slow furnace cooling after processing to coarsen the microstructure
Cold rolling the sheet at room temperature to raise dislocation density
Controlled rolling and cooling to refine the ferrite grain size

rubric: Strain hardening and grain refinement both obstruct dislocation motion and raise yield strength.
Recrystallisation, grain growth and coarsening all soften the steel.

items.prompt: A designer is building a unidirectional glass/epoxy panel with a fibre volume fraction of 0.5. The glass fibres have E = 72 GPa and the epoxy matrix has E = 3 GPa. The load acts along the fibre direction and the fibres are well bonded. What is the best estimate of the panel's modulus in that direction?

options.label: 75.0 GPa
37.5 GPa
24.0 GPa
5.8 GPa

rubric: Along the fibres the rule of mixtures gives E = 0.5(72) + 0.5(3) = 37.5 GPa.
5.8 GPa is the transverse (series) estimate, which applies only to loading across the fibres.

items.prompt: A welded carbon-steel tank passed room-temperature tensile tests but cracked on a freezing night, leaving a flat, shiny fracture surface with almost no visible deformation. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Cold converted the ferrite to martensite, which is hard and brittle throughout the tank wall
Its BCC structure has a ductile-to-brittle transition, so below it slip is hard and cracks run unchecked
Low temperature formed creep voids along grain boundaries, which linked into a flat fracture
Contraction at low temperature raised the modulus enough to exceed the ultimate tensile strength

rubric: BCC steels lose slip mobility at low temperature, so fracture switches from ductile to cleavage.
Martensite does not form on cooling to ambient low temperatures, and creep needs high temperature.

items.prompt: Nickel alloy turbine blades slowly lengthen over months at 900 C (about 0.6 of melting temperature in K) under a stress well below their room-temperature yield strength. What best explains this?

options.label: Fatigue cracks grow at each start-up, and the opened cracks add to the blade's length
Thermal expansion at high temperature stretches the blade permanently once held long enough
Diffusion and dislocation climb allow time-dependent plastic strain even below the yield stress
Oxide scale forms on the surface, and its weight pulls the blade longer under gravity

rubric: Creep at high homologous temperature is thermally activated and occurs below the yield stress.
Thermal expansion is reversible, and fatigue cracks or oxide do not produce steady elongation.

items.prompt: At 20 C a PMMA sample (Tg about 105 C) fractures with little deformation, but a polyethylene sample (Tg far below 0 C) bends and yields. Which analysis explains the difference?

options.label: PMMA is below its Tg, so chains are frozen, while polyethylene's amorphous regions are above Tg and can move
Polyethylene is highly crystalline, and its ordered crystals slip more readily than the disordered chains of a glassy polymer
Polyethylene has stronger covalent bonds along its backbone than PMMA, so its chains resist breaking when bent
PMMA is crosslinked into a rigid network, whereas polyethylene is a linear thermoplastic whose chains slide freely

rubric: Below Tg chain segments cannot move, so the polymer is glassy and brittle; above Tg they flow and absorb energy.
PMMA is a linear thermoplastic and polyethylene is only partly crystalline, so the other options misread the structure.

items.prompt: Identical alumina bars give flexural strengths from 280 to 420 MPa, although processing and composition were the same. Which diagnosis best explains the scatter?

options.label: Different bars contain different slip systems, so dislocation glide differs from bar to bar
Strength depends on the size of the largest flaw in each bar, and flaw sizes vary randomly between bars
Residual moisture in the bars changes their atomic bond type, giving a different modulus for each
Alumina yields plastically by a variable amount, so each bar work-hardens by a different degree

rubric: Brittle ceramics fail from the most severe pre-existing flaw (Griffith), so strengths scatter statistically.
Alumina has almost no dislocation plasticity at room temperature, so work hardening and slip explanations fail.

items.prompt: Steel bolts fasten an aluminium plate on a boat in seawater. After a year, pitting appears in the plate around each bolt. What explains this?

options.label: Steel is more reactive than aluminium, so the bolts dissolve and deposit corrosion products on the plate
The bolts are stronger than the plate, so stress concentrates around them and drives stress-corrosion cracking
Seawater dissolves the passive layer on the steel, which then pulls electrons away from the whole plate evenly
Aluminium is anodic to steel, so in the seawater electrolyte it corrodes preferentially where it touches the bolts

rubric: In a galvanic couple the more anodic metal (aluminium) corrodes near the contact, with seawater completing the circuit.
Reactivity of iron versus aluminium is the wrong way round here, and uniform attack would not give local pitting.

items.prompt: A brass strip was cold rolled heavily and then cracked when bent. Which factors explain its loss of ductility? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rolling already relieved internal stress by recrystallising the grains into a softer state
Dislocation density has risen sharply, so dislocations obstruct each other's glide
Rolling changed the brass into a different crystal structure by phase transformation
Dislocation tangles and cell walls leave little capacity for further plastic strain

rubric: Strain hardening raises dislocation density and entanglement, which uses up ductility.
Cold rolling does not change the crystal structure, and recrystallisation only happens on annealing.

items.prompt: A steel drive shaft broke in service. The fracture surface shows smooth, curved beach marks that start at the corner of a keyway, with a small rough zone on the opposite side. Which interpretation best fits the evidence?

options.label: Fatigue crack growth began at the keyway stress concentration, and the small rough zone is the final fast fracture
A single torsional overload twisted the shaft past its ultimate strength, giving the smooth curved marks
Creep rupture at high temperature produced the beach marks, with the small rough zone as oxide scale
Brittle impact cleavage began at the keyway, and the beach marks show repeated impact blows over time

rubric: Beach marks from an origin at a stress raiser, plus a small final fracture zone, indicate fatigue under low nominal stress.
Overload fractures lack beach marks and creep needs high temperature.

items.prompt: A cold-drawn copper wire is annealed for 1 h at 250°C: its hardness barely changes but its resistivity falls noticeably. At 400°C its hardness drops by about half. Which account fits both observations?

options.label: Stress relief at 250°C healed the grain boundaries and lowered resistivity; at 400°C surface oxidation made the wire softer overall
Grain growth at 250°C coarsened the grains and lowered resistivity; at 400°C precipitates dissolved and removed the strengthening phase
Recovery at 250°C cut point defects and dislocation strain, lowering resistivity; recrystallization at 400°C replaced the hard deformed grains
A phase change at 250°C reduced dislocation density and lowered resistivity; at 400°C twinning replaced the deformed grains with softer crystals

rubric: Recovery lowers point defects and rearranges dislocations, which cuts resistivity while hardness stays high; recrystallization then removes the stored dislocation structure and softens the wire.
Distractors invent precipitates, grain growth or phase changes that pure copper does not undergo at these temperatures.

items.prompt: A steel shaft under rotating bending fails after about 10^7 cycles. The nominal stress was below the endurance limit, and beach marks radiate from a sharp keyway corner. Which analysis best explains the failure?

options.label: The sharp corner concentrated stress above the endurance limit locally, starting a crack that grew cycle by cycle
Beach marks show brittle cleavage from low temperature, so the cyclic loading played little part in the failure at the keyway
The shaft yielded in bulk on the first cycle, and the crack then spread by plastic collapse across the whole section of the shaft
The nominal stress was below the endurance limit, so a void left from manufacturing in the keyway must have caused the failure

rubric: The stress concentration at the corner raises local cyclic stress above the endurance limit even though the nominal stress is below it, and beach marks show fatigue crack growth.
Distractors ignore stress concentration or confuse fatigue with overload or cleavage.

items.prompt: A polycarbonate housing passes inspection but cracks at a screw boss only after being wiped with a cleaning solvent. The cracks start at the surface. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.label: Solvent raised the glass transition temperature, making the polymer glassy and brittle once stress was applied to it
Solvent reacted with the carbon backbone, severing chains throughout the part and uniformly lowering its molar mass
Solvent absorbed at the surface plasticised the amorphous polymer, letting crazes form under residual moulding stress
Solvent dissolved the crystalline regions, which removed the load-bearing phase and caused ductile tearing at the boss

rubric: This is environmental stress cracking: a solvent plus residual or applied tensile stress nucleates crazes in an amorphous polymer.
Distractors assume crystallinity, bulk chain scission or a rise in Tg, none of which explains surface-initiated cracking at a stress raiser.

items.prompt: An Al-Cu alloy aged at 190°C reaches peak hardness at 18 h. A sample held for 200 h at the same temperature is much softer, though the alloy composition is unchanged. What best explains the softening?

options.label: Grain boundaries disappeared during the long hold, so Hall-Petch strengthening was lost across the whole of the sample
Dislocation density rose during the long hold, and the extra dislocations made slip easier across the grains of the alloy
Precipitates coarsened and spread apart, so dislocations bow between them or bypass them at a much lower stress
Solute went back into solution at 190°C, so the matrix lost its supersaturation and the precipitates vanished entirely

rubric: Overaging coarsens precipitates and widens their spacing, so dislocations pass more easily and strength falls.
Distractors claim dissolution, extra dislocations or grain-boundary loss, none of which occurs at constant aging temperature.

items.prompt: Flexural tests on 30 alumina bars give strengths from 220 to 410 MPa, while 30 steel bars vary by under 5%. Which analysis best explains the spread in the ceramic?

options.label: Alumina is anisotropic at the atomic scale, so each bar's strength depends on the orientation of a single crystal
Alumina fails from the most severe flaw in each bar and cannot yield to blunt it, so strength follows flaw size
Alumina has a lower elastic modulus than steel, so each bar deflects differently before reaching its stress limit
Alumina bars contain more dislocations than steel, and their motion differs between bars and so changes the strength

rubric: Brittle ceramics fail from the largest flaw, whose size varies between bars, and with no plasticity to blunt crack tips the scatter is large.
Distractors point to dislocation motion, modulus or single-crystal orientation, which do not explain the flaw-controlled scatter.

items.prompt: Cracks appear in the heat-affected zone of a weld in a high-strength low-alloy steel a day after welding, with no external load. Which factors combine to cause this delayed cracking? Select all that apply.

options.label: Compressive residual stress introduced by peening of the weld toe
A fully pearlitic microstructure formed by very slow cooling after welding
Residual tensile stress from weld shrinkage as the joint cools
A hard martensitic microstructure formed by rapid cooling of the heat-affected zone
Dissolved hydrogen picked up from moisture in the electrode coating

rubric: Hydrogen cracking needs a susceptible hard microstructure, hydrogen and tensile stress together.
Pearlite is less susceptible and compressive stress suppresses crack opening, so those options work against cracking.

items.prompt: A unidirectional carbon-epoxy coupon fails at 1800 MPa when loaded along the fibres. A coupon cut at 30° to the fibres fails near 120 MPa, with the fracture running parallel to the fibres. A technician suspects poor fibre quality. What does the analysis show?

options.label: Off-axis load puts shear and transverse stress on the weak matrix and interface, so failure follows the fibres; fibre quality is not implicated
Fibres carry less load at every angle because carbon is weak in tension, so the result confirms poor fibre quality
Off-axis load raises the fibre volume fraction in the loaded section, which lowers stiffness and so the failure stress
The epoxy is stronger than the fibres in shear, so shear at 30° loads the fibres in compression and buckles them

rubric: Unidirectional composites are strongly anisotropic: off-axis loading resolves into matrix-dominated shear and transverse stresses, so failure runs along the fibres.
Distractors blame fibre quality or invent mechanisms that do not match a fracture running parallel to the fibres.

items.prompt: Choose the material giving the lightest solid square-section beam of fixed length for a required bending stiffness; ignore cost and corrosion. The merit index is E^(1/2)/density. Candidates (E in GPa, density in g/cm^3): steel 210, 7.8; Al alloy 70, 2.7; Ti alloy 110, 4.5; Mg alloy 45, 1.74.

options.label: Magnesium alloy
Titanium alloy
Steel
Aluminium alloy

rubric: The index values are about 1.86 for steel, 3.10 for Al, 2.33 for Ti and 3.86 for Mg, so Mg gives the lightest beam.
Choosing steel, Al or Ti comes from using E or E/density, which suits ties rather than bending beams.

items.prompt: A gear needs a wear-resistant surface and a core that survives shock loads. Judging against these two criteria, which processing route is best?

options.label: Cold-work a low-carbon steel heavily, which hardens the surface most because strain concentrates at the outside of the part
Anneal a medium-carbon steel to a coarse pearlite structure, which gives good toughness with moderate hardness throughout
Through-harden a high-carbon steel by quenching and light tempering to give uniform high hardness everywhere in the tooth
Carburise low-carbon steel and quench, giving a hard high-carbon case over a tough low-carbon core

rubric: Case hardening gives a hard wear surface and a tough core, meeting both criteria.
Through-hardened high-carbon steel is brittle under shock, and annealing or cold work cannot give a hard case with a tough core.

items.prompt: A moulded clip must survive thousands of cycles of 5% bending strain at room temperature without cracking. Judge which material best meets this requirement.

options.label: Polystyrene, a glassy amorphous polymer whose high stiffness and good flex endurance suit repeated strain
Phenolic, a crosslinked thermoset whose rigid network resists fatigue crack growth under large cyclic strains
Polypropylene, a semi-crystalline polymer whose ductile crystalline-amorphous structure absorbs large flexing
PMMA, a glassy polymer whose clarity and surface hardness give it a high strain to failure when flexed

rubric: Semi-crystalline polypropylene is ductile at room temperature and withstands repeated flexing, as in living hinges.
Polystyrene, phenolic and PMMA are rigid and brittle, with low strain to failure under cyclic bending.

items.prompt: For ferritic steel brackets used at -40°C, an engineer proposes further hardening to raise yield strength and so prevent brittle fracture. Judge this proposal.

options.label: Flawed: more hardening usually lowers toughness and raises the transition temperature, so grain refining or nickel suits better
Flawed: ferritic steels stay ductile at any temperature, so the real risk is creep, which hardening would make worse
Sound: hardening shifts the transition temperature below -40°C because the stronger lattice resists cleavage at low temperatures
Sound: higher yield strength means a higher load before plastic flow, so cracks cannot grow and brittle fracture is prevented

rubric: Strengthening by hardening generally reduces toughness and raises the ductile-brittle transition temperature, whereas fine grains and nickel lower it.
Distractors confuse strength with toughness or claim ferritic steels never turn brittle.

items.prompt: Assemblies in seawater are joined with fasteners of different metals. Judging the risk of rapid galvanic attack on the fastener, which assembly is worst?

options.label: Aluminium rivets joining large stainless steel sheets, giving a small anode and a large cathode in contact
Aluminium rivets joining large aluminium sheets, giving matching metals and no potential difference to drive attack
Stainless steel bolts joining large aluminium plates, giving a small cathode and a large anode in contact
Stainless steel bolts joining large stainless sheets, giving matching metals and no potential difference to drive attack

rubric: A small anode against a large cathode concentrates the corrosion current on the anode, so the aluminium rivets corrode quickly.
The stainless-bolt-in-aluminium case is the reverse area ratio, which spreads attack thinly, and the matching-metal cases have no galvanic driving force.

items.prompt: Judge which choices are sound for resisting creep in a jet-engine turbine blade operating near 0.8 of its absolute melting temperature. Select all that apply.

options.label: Single-crystal blades remove grain boundaries, where sliding and diffusion drive creep at high temperature
A ceramic thermal barrier coating with internal cooling lowers the metal temperature, cutting the creep rate
A very fine grain size gives the best creep resistance, since more boundaries always block deformation at high temperature
A low-melting alloy suits the blade, as lower bonding energy makes atoms diffuse less readily when hot
Gamma-prime precipitates in a nickel superalloy resist dislocation motion and stay stable at high temperature

rubric: Removing boundaries, stable coherent precipitates and lowering the metal temperature all reduce creep.
Fine grains speed boundary sliding at high temperature, and low-melting alloys diffuse faster at a given temperature.

items.prompt: A hip stem must resist fatigue, resist corrosion in body fluid, and limit stress shielding of the femur (bone E about 20 GPa) by being as compliant as possible. Candidates, with E in GPa: CoCr alloy 210, 316L steel 190, Ti-6Al-4V 110, alumina 380 (brittle). Which best meets the stated criteria?

options.label: Ti-6Al-4V, as it is the most compliant viable option with good corrosion and fatigue resistance
Alumina, as its very high stiffness and chemical inertness keep the stem from deforming under cyclic loads
316L steel, as its modulus is close to that of bone and it resists crevice corrosion in body fluid very well
CoCr alloy, as its high stiffness carries load well and its corrosion and fatigue resistance are excellent in service

rubric: Ti-6Al-4V has the lowest modulus among the viable options while meeting corrosion and fatigue needs, so it limits stress shielding best.
CoCr and 316L are much stiffer than bone, 316L's modulus is not close to bone's, and brittle alumina with the highest stiffness worsens stress shielding.

items.prompt: A panel of fixed length and width must reach a target bending stiffness at minimum mass, with thickness free to vary. Which material index should be maximised to rank candidates?

options.label: E/rho

rubric: For a stiffness-limited panel with free thickness, mass scales so the index is E^(1/3)/rho.
E/rho applies to ties and E^(1/2)/rho to solid beams; learners misapply those.

items.prompt: An engineer says dense alumina should reach a tensile strength near E/10 because its bonds are strong, so a measured 300 MPa shows poor processing. Which critique is best?

options.label: Strength is set by the largest flaw through K_IC/(Y sqrt(pi a)), so 300 MPa is typical and scatter needs Weibull statistics
Alumina yields plastically at room temperature, so the measured value reflects flow that processing barely changes
The E/10 estimate holds only for amorphous ceramics, since grain boundaries in crystalline ones always cut strength
Bond strength limits only compressive loading, so tensile tests on ceramics say little about their usable design strength

rubric: Brittle fracture is flaw-controlled (Griffith), so real strength is far below the theoretical value.
Distractors wrongly invoke plasticity or amorphous structure.

items.prompt: A Sn-Pb solder joint (melting about 183 C, 456 K) in a room-temperature electronics unit carries steady modest load plus thermal cycling. Which failure mode should be assessed first?

options.label: Oxidation scaling, since solder sits far above a safe homologous temperature in air
Creep and thermomechanical fatigue, since 295 K is about 0.65 of the melting point
Stress corrosion cracking, since tin passive films crack under static load in dry air
Brittle cleavage, since low-melting alloys are BCC and lose toughness at room temperature

rubric: Homologous temperature above about 0.5 makes creep significant, and cycling adds fatigue.
The cleavage distractor misapplies the BCC ductile-brittle transition.

items.prompt: A transmission gear needs surface hardness above 58 HRC for wear and a tough core for shock loads, and is made from 0.2% C steel. Which process best meets both criteria?

options.label: Cold-work the gear heavily, since strain hardening hardens the surface while the core stays tough
Anneal fully, since ferrite-pearlite gives uniform toughness and the best wear resistance
Through-harden by quenching from austenite, since 0.2% C steel reaches 58 HRC at every depth
Carburise, then quench and temper, giving a hard high-carbon martensitic case over a tough low-carbon core

rubric: Carburising raises surface carbon so only the case becomes hard martensite.
Low-carbon martensite cannot reach 58 HRC, and annealing or cold work cannot give a graded case.

items.prompt: A space mirror substrate must minimise steady-state thermal distortion under a heat flux, so the criterion is to maximise k/alpha. Which material ranks best?

options.label: Borosilicate glass (k 1.1 W/mK, alpha 3.3 ppm/K)
Invar (k 10 W/mK, alpha 1.3 ppm/K)
Aluminium alloy (k 200 W/mK, alpha 23 ppm/K)
Silicon carbide (k 150 W/mK, alpha 4 ppm/K)

rubric: k/alpha is about 37 for SiC, 9 for aluminium, 8 for Invar and 0.3 for glass.
Invar is tempting for low alpha alone but its low conductivity gives steep gradients.

items.prompt: A team proposes grain refinement to extend creep life of a turbine blade operating above 0.7 of its absolute melting point. Which statements are valid critiques? Select all that apply.

options.label: Grain-boundary sliding and diffusion creep speed up as boundary area rises, so finer grains usually shorten creep life
Directional solidification or single crystals remove transverse boundaries and are the usual approach at this temperature
Grain size has no effect on diffusion creep, so only precipitate content matters at high temperature
Hall-Petch strengthening works mainly at low homologous temperature, where boundaries block dislocations
Finer grains lower yield strength at every temperature, so refinement is never used for strengthening

rubric: At high homologous temperature boundaries are weak paths, so creep-resistant blades minimise them.
The last two options deny grain-size effects that exist.

items.prompt: A pressure vessel with 20 mm wall must leak before it breaks. Design stress is 0.5 of yield and the geometry factor Y is 1. Steel A: yield 900 MPa, K_IC 50 MPa sqrt(m). Steel B: yield 600 MPa, K_IC 120 MPa sqrt(m). Which steel meets leak-before-break?

options.label: Steel B, because its lower yield strength gives more ductility, so any crack in it will blunt and leak before fracture
Steel A, because its higher design stress of 450 MPa lets a crack arrest at a larger size than in the other steel
Steel B, because its critical flaw (about 50 mm) exceeds the wall thickness, so a through-crack leaks first
Steel A, because its higher strength allows a thinner wall, so the critical flaw is smaller than the thickness

rubric: a_c = (1/pi)(K/sigma)^2 gives about 4 mm for A (below 20 mm) and about 51 mm for B.
Distractors confuse strength with crack tolerance or cite ductility without calculation.

items.prompt: A SiC-fibre/SiC-matrix combustor liner must fail non-catastrophically, unlike monolithic ceramic, and survive oxidising heat. Which fibre-matrix interface design meets this?

options.label: A strong chemical bond between fibre and matrix, so load transfers fully and cracks run straight through
No interface layer, with fibre and matrix of equal modulus, so stress concentrates nowhere in the part
A thin weak carbon or BN coating on the fibres, so matrix cracks deflect and fibres debond and pull out
A thick ductile polymer coating on the fibres, so they slide freely at every combustion temperature

rubric: A weak interface gives crack deflection, debonding and fibre pull-out, so toughness rises.
A strong bond gives brittle failure and a polymer coating would burn away.

items.prompt: A plan to strengthen a cast Al-4Cu part says: heat to 190 C, hold 8 h, air cool, put in service. Which essential step does the plan omit for precipitation hardening?

options.label: Preheating to the eutectic temperature to partly melt grain boundaries, which homogenises the copper before the ageing hold
Solution treatment above the solvus, then a rapid quench to a supersaturated solid solution
Cold work after ageing to dissolve the precipitates and raise dislocation density, so strain hardening replaces precipitate strengthening
Slow furnace cooling from the melt to grow large equilibrium CuAl2 particles, which block dislocations and raise hardness

rubric: Without solution treatment and quench there is no supersaturation, so ageing gives coarse equilibrium phases.
Other options describe steps that soften or damage the alloy.

items.prompt: Design a mouldable polymer composite for an electronics heat spreader that must be electrically insulating and thermally conductive. Which filler plan meets all constraints?

options.label: Short glass fibres at high loading, to raise stiffness and so conduct heat better
Boron nitride or aluminium nitride particles above the thermal percolation loading in epoxy
Copper flakes at high loading, to form low-resistance heat paths through the matrix
Carbon black above the electrical percolation threshold, forming conductive networks

rubric: BN and AlN are electrical insulators with high thermal conductivity, so they satisfy both constraints.
Carbon black and copper make the composite conduct electricity; glass fibre barely raises conductivity.

items.prompt: A 304 stainless tank must be field-welded with no chance of post-weld solution annealing, and the heat-affected zone must resist intergranular corrosion. Which change meets this?

options.label: Specify low-carbon 304L or Ti-stabilised 321, so little chromium carbide forms at the boundaries
Specify high-carbon 304H, so more carbides form early and pin the boundaries in the heat-affected zone
Cool the weld slowly through 500-800 C, so chromium diffuses back in and heals the boundary depletion
Preheat the plate to 600 C, so carbon dissolves into the matrix and never reaches the grain boundaries

rubric: Low carbon or stabilisers prevent Cr23C6 precipitation, avoiding sensitisation without heat treatment.
Slow cooling or higher carbon worsens sensitisation.

items.prompt: Design a carbon/epoxy laminate that has equal in-plane stiffness in all directions and does not warp after cure. Which stacking sequence meets both requirements?
rubric: Equal 0/45/-45/90 plies are quasi-isotropic, and the mirror-symmetric layup removes bending-extension coupling.
The unsymmetric layup warps; the cross-ply options are not quasi-isotropic.

items.prompt: A steel shaft with a stepped shoulder fails in rotating-bending fatigue. Design changes must raise its endurance limit without changing the material or shaft diameters. Which measures meet this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Increase the fillet radius at the shoulder to reduce the stress concentration factor
Hard-chrome plate the shoulder, since a hard layer always blocks crack initiation
Grind and polish the shoulder to remove machining marks that start cracks
Through-harden to maximum hardness, since higher strength always raises the endurance limit
Shot-peen the shoulder to introduce compressive residual stress at the surface

rubric: Peening, larger radii and a better finish all cut crack initiation at the notch.
Chrome plating can add tensile stress and cracks, and very hard steel is notch-sensitive.

items.prompt: A hip-implant stem must carry cyclic body loads for decades, resist corrosion in body fluid, be biocompatible, and have a stiffness close to bone (about 20 GPa) to limit stress shielding. Which candidate best meets the constraints as a whole?

options.label: A cobalt-chromium alloy (E about 230 GPa), for the highest wear and strength
A dense alumina ceramic (E about 380 GPa), for inertness and hardness
A 316L stainless steel (E about 195 GPa), for low cost and easy machining
A beta-titanium alloy (E about 70 GPa), with a stable passive oxide film

rubric: Beta-titanium has the lowest modulus of the options while staying strong, corrosion-resistant and biocompatible.
The other options are much stiffer, and alumina is also brittle under cyclic bending.
